extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and mathematics students who write proofs (authors of mathematical proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing mathematical proofs using hierarchical structuring, explicit naming, and formal-proof-inspired constructs (assume/prove, suffices, pick, case) to improve clarity and reduce errors. Covers both informal typeset proofs and practices that support machine-checkable proofs (TLA+/TLAPS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Add hierarchical structuring to proofs so that the function of each assertion is clear and additional explanation does not obscure the larger picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sequence-of-named-statements with proofs for steps; structure makes it clear whether a sentence asserts a new fact or justifies a previous assertion; structured proofs let you add detail without hiding the overall logic. (From: "Making proofs easier to understand is easy. It requires only the simple application of two principles: structure and naming.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Name all facts, assumptions, and intermediate statements so the reader can tell exactly which are being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give names to the interval, assumptions, and steps (e.g., name the interval I, use step numbers like 1, 1.1, etc.). Refer to named assumptions explicitly in proofs instead of relying on readers to infer them. (From: "Naming all facts makes it easy to tell the reader exactly which ones are being used.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Final step must state the goal (Q.E.D.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The last step of every proof should be the statement of what the proof is trying to prove (or an explicit Q.E.D. step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not end a proof with an assertion that is not the theorem's conclusion; change the last step to Q.E.D. or restate the goal so the proof explicitly shows it reached the objective. (From: "The style requires that the last step of every proof be a statement of what it is that the proof is trying to prove ... we write Q.E.D.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify choices and existence (pick/choose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the proof 'chooses' an object (e.g., 'let a and b be...'), justify the existence of such an object within the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce picks as steps (pick x ∈ S : P(x)) and provide subproofs that such an x exists. Do not rely on implicit existential choices in prose. (From: "When we choose something in a proof, we have to prove that it exists.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Make assumption scope explicit (ASSUME/PROVE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an assume/prove construct to declare assumptions and to make their scope explicit, rather than leaving assumptions implicit in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write theorem statements and intermediate steps as assume/prove so assumptions apply only where intended. Explain that ordinary prose assertions can be interpreted as assume/prove at the theorem level but are ambiguous inside proofs. (From: section on ASSUME/PROVE.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'suffices' to change the current goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a suffices construct to replace the current goal with a simpler or more convenient subgoal, carrying along assumptions for the remainder of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffices steps change the current goal (e.g., 'suffices assume ... prove ...'); they can simplify structure and avoid extra proof levels. Note that any suffices can be eliminated by restructuring, and that a good level of 4–10 steps per level aids readability. (From: section on SUFFICES and examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical numbering and local referencing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Number steps hierarchically (e.g., 3.3.4) and enforce locality so references to step names always mean the most recent preceding step with that name and do not violate hierarchical scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid illegal cross-level references (e.g., don't refer to step 2.4.1 from inside proof of 3.3.4 if assumptions differ). Use a numbering/visibility scheme where only certain preceding steps are valid references. (From: section 4.2 Hierarchical Numbering.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep level sizes readable
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize proofs so each hierarchical level contains a manageable number of steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for about 4 to 10 steps per level; removing or adding 'suffices' changes levels and can improve readability. Very deep numbering becomes hard to read—use indentation and hypertext to manage detail. (From: "Proofs are generally easiest to read if each level contains about 4 to 10 steps.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly cite used theorems and lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: When a step depends on another theorem or lemma, state that dependence and, if necessary, the justification that the theorem's hypotheses hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit the chain of reasons (e.g., differentiability implies continuity): when using the Mean Value Theorem, explicitly show why its hypotheses are met rather than assuming readers will fill the gap. (From discussion of child asking 'Why?' and the expansion in Figure 4.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide subproof detail but allow skipping
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide as much detailed explanation as needed to be convincing, but structure it so readers can skip lower-level detail and still see the big picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indentation/hierarchical steps and, when available, hypertext to let readers hide/show proofs of individual steps; include more detail for less sophisticated audiences or when any doubt exists. (From: "Proper structuring allows us to add as much detailed explanation as we like without obscuring the larger picture.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof sketches (comments) for intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert proof sketches or comments between a statement and its proof to explain the intuition or highlight key ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sketches at any hierarchical level so a reader uninterested in formal details can read the sketch and skip the rest; with hypertext, comments can be attached and hidden as needed. (From: Section 4.4 Comments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equational reasoning usage and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use equational proofs (sequences of relations) when appropriate for elegance, but be aware of their limitations on paper regarding hierarchical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equational proofs are elegant and work well as lowest-level arguments where each relation's justification is short. On paper they can be awkward to display with hierarchical subproofs; hypertext handles this better. (From: Section 4.3 Equational Proofs and Figure 5.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Express case analyses as structured 'case F' steps (abbreviations for assume F / prove Q.E.D.), followed by a Q.E.D. that shows cases are exhaustive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sequence of case steps and then Q.E.D., citing the case statements and demonstrating exhaustiveness; it's easy to express in prose but cleaner to write as 'case n ≥ 0' etc. (From: section on CASE.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Local definitions as proof steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce local definitions inside a proof as steps; the definition is in effect for the rest of the current proof level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single step can contain multiple definitions. Use this to name expressions or simplify later steps, keeping scope explicit. (From: 'Definitions' subsection.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal proof languages and machine checking where practical
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalizing proofs in a language (e.g., TLA+) and using a prover (e.g., TLAPS) is ideal for ensuring correctness, and learning formal proofs can improve informal proof writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completely formal, machine-checked proofs are the Platonic ideal. While full machine-checked proofs are currently costly, teaching formal proofs is valuable; the author uses TLA+ and TLAPS examples. (From: Section 4.5.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ruthlessly suspicious; fill non-obvious gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: If the truth of a statement is not completely obvious, provide the necessary detail—do not trust intuition when writing a proof intended to avoid errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagine a child asking 'Why?' at every assertion; write out proofs of steps whose correctness is even slightly doubtful. This helps catch omissions and errors that prose often conceals. (From: 'The best way I know to eliminate errors...' and related passages.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor level of detail to audience sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose how much explanation to include based on the reader: beginning students need more detail than expert mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing to show correctness to others, include more steps; if writing for oneself, include detail whenever any doubt exists. Use structured proofs to provide optional detail for different readers. (From: 'How much detail is necessary? ... depends on the sophistication of the reader.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implicit assumptions and ambiguous scope in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on prose's implicit scopes for assumptions and variable meanings—make scopes explicit to prevent confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prose often leaves unclear whether a sentence asserts a new fact or justifies a prior one; use hierarchical structuring and assume/prove to make scope explicit and avoid readers needing to read the whole proof to justify the first sentence. (From: introductory discussion and ASSUME/PROVE section.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hypertext/features of tools to manage verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, present structured proofs with hypertext or tool support so readers can view only the desired level of detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-line viewers (e.g., TLA+ Toolbox) let readers open/hide subproofs; for printed text rely on indentation and numbering but consider putting long formal proofs online with a sketch in the paper. (From: multiple passages about hypertext and the TLA+ Toolbox.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and notation conventions for structured proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt compact, formal-looking constructs (assume/prove, suffices, pick, case, Q.E.D.) and adopt consistent numbering/notation to replace verbose prose phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce these keywords to readers (or use them informally) to convey structure succinctly; consider adopting compact notation instead of lengthy phrases like 'We now consider the case in which...'. (From: 'It seems safer to introduce assume and prove as keywords...' and related guidance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish proof sketch from proof (separate explanation from formal argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a short proof sketch to explain the key ideas, while keeping the formal structured proof separate and explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches help readers understand intuition; structured proofs allow aligning sketches with formal steps, unlike prose where it's hard to relate sketch to details. (From: objections section and comments on proof sketches.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on logical structure over literary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's value lies in its logical structure, not in literary quality; prioritize clarity and correctness over elegant prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't try to make proofs 'great literature'; use structure to express beauty of mathematics. (From: 'A proof should be great literature.' objection and rebuttal.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When mechanizing proofs, decompose for the prover (cite used facts/defs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the goal is machine-checkability, decompose proofs into low-level steps that cite which definitions and facts are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowest-level paragraphs should state which facts and definitions are used to aid automated provers (as done in the appendix TLA+ formal proof). The decomposition may be for the prover's benefit rather than for human readers. (From appendix discussion of TLAPS decomposition.)
